newsitem.title: PERU: Peru to "evaluate" renewing talks with rebels.
newsitem.headline: Peru to "evaluate" renewing talks with rebels.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori said on Tuesday Peru's government would "evaluate" the renewal of stalled talks with Marxist rebels holding 72 captives for 12 weeks at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima.

Fujimori insisted in a radio interview that he would "exhaust" all non-violent methods to solve the hostage crisis, but could not say when direct negotiations with the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) might resume.

At an imminent meeting between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and guarantors overseeing the talks' process, "an evaluation will be made to see at what moment these conversations can be restarted," Fujimori said.

"I repeat and I insist that we will always exhaust all the peaceful measures at our disposition and we hope that the same conduct is maintained -- that is to say, that there are no victims inside the embassy."
The president refused to confirm or deny the existence of a tunnel under the residence, which the MRTA had said caused it to call off talks last week to end the hostage crisis.

"Obviously the state cannot reveal what are its working plans, its strategy to handle this problem caused by the MRTA," Fujimori said. "I am not going to say if there is a tunnel or tunnels. I am not going to say if there are airborne commandos prepared or if we have commandos who could work with paralysing gases or other methods."

The rebels boycotted a 10th round of talks scheduled for last Friday, alleging the tunnel was part of a plan to storm the residence while MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa and his second-in-command Rolly Rojas were at negotiations in a safe house across the road.

Despite Fujimori's comments, his Defence Minister Tomas Meza Castillo has denied the existence of a tunnel. Yet some security force sources have said at least four tunnels were being built, and two local newspapers have published photographs and diagrams backing up the MRTA's claim.

Although the MRTA agreed to restart talks on Monday, Palermo decided not to attend. Some analysts viewed this as a retaliatory measure by a government piqued at both the rebels' first suspension of talks and their earlier refusal of an asylum offer from Cuba.

"Minister Palermo has been very clear. He has said that the conditions are not right for this dialogue to have results," said Fujimori, explaining his negotiatior's decision. "We believe that it is not the MRTA group which is going to fix the conditions for this conversation. The government is going to persist in getting positive results and not just conversations."

While the approximately 20 rebels inside the residence remained silent on Tuesday other than singing their revolutionary anthem at dawn, the MRTA's international office in Hamburg issued a statement reiterating the group's central demand for the release of more than 400 jailed comrades.

"Three months after the takeover of the residence, the situation is virtually the same as in the first days. We cannot see clearly the government's peaceful option and, on the contrary, Fujimori still keeps playing the military option," the statement said. "This obviously puts in danger the lives of the people inside."

In Tokyo, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was concerned by Monday's latest cancellation of talks and that his bad premonitions about the progress of events had been born out. "I had a feeling that there would be consequences. And so there were," he said.

The MRTA released most of their captives within a few days of the takeover but are still holding 72, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, two government ministers and an all-star list of Japanese businessmen.
